title: Latin literature
wiki_lead:
Latin literature includes the essays, histories, poems, plays, and other writings written in the Latin language. The beginning of formal Latin literature dates to 240 BC, when the first stage play in Latin was performed in Atella, a town in Campania south of Rome. Latin literature flourished for the next six centuries. The classical era of Latin literature can be roughly divided into several periods: early Latin literature, the golden age, the imperial period and Late Antiquity.
Latin was the language of the ancient Romans as well as being the lingua franca of Western and Central Europe throughout the Middle Ages. Latin literature features the work of Roman authors, such as Cicero, Virgil, Ovid and Horace, but also includes the work of European writers after the fall of the Empire, from religious writers like Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) to secular writers like Francis Bacon (1561–1626), Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), and Isaac Newton (1642–1727).

History


Early Latin literature

Although literature in Latin followed a continual development over several centuries, the beginnings of formal Latin literature started with the regular performance of comedies and tragedies in Rome in 240 BC, one year after the conclusion of the First Punic War. These initial comedies and tragedies were adapted from Greek drama by Livius Andronicus, a Greek prisoner of war who had been brought to Rome as a slave in 272 BC. Andronicus translated Homer's Odyssey into Latin using a traditional Latin verse form called Saturnian meter. In 235 BC, Gnaeus Naevius, a Roman citizen, continued this tradition of producing dramas that were reworkings of Greek originals, or fabula palliata, and he expanded on this by producing a new type of drama, fabula praetexta, or tragedies based on Roman myths and history, starting in 222 BC. Later in life, Naevius composed an epic poem in Saturnian meter on the first Punic War, in which he had fought.
Other epic poets followed Naevius. Quintus Ennius wrote an historical epic, the Annals (soon after 200 BC), describing Roman history from the founding of Rome to his own time. He adopted the Greek dactylic hexameter, which became the standard verse form for Roman epics. He became well known for his tragic dramas. Successors in this field include Marcus Pacuvius and Lucius Accius. These three writers rarely used episodes from Roman history, but they wrote Latin versions of tragic themes that the Greeks had already written about. Even when they copied the Greeks, their translations were not straightforward replicas of the original Greek works. Only fragments of their plays have survived.

Considerably more is known about early Latin comedy, as 26 Early Latin comedies are extant – 20 of which were written by Plautus; the remaining six were written by Terence. These men modeled their comedies on Greek plays known as New Comedy, but treated the plots and wording of the originals freely. Plautus scattered songs throughout his plays and added to the humor with puns and wisecracks, as well as comic actions by the actors. Terence's plays were more austere in tone, dealing with domestic situations. His works provided the chief inspiration for French and English comedies of the 17th century AD.
The prose of the period is best known through On Agriculture (160 BC) by Cato the Elder. Cato wrote the first Latin history of Rome and of other Italian cities. He was the first Roman statesman to put his political speeches in writing as a means of influencing public opinion.
Early Latin literature ended with Gaius Lucilius, who created a new kind of poetry in his 30 books of Satires (2nd century BC). He wrote in an easy, conversational tone about books, food, friends, and current events.


The golden age

grok_lead: Latin literature encompasses the body of written works in the Latin language, originating in ancient Rome during the 3rd century BCE and extending through the medieval, Renaissance, and modern periods up to the present day, including poetry, prose, drama, historiography, philosophy, and religious texts that profoundly shaped Western intellectual and cultural traditions. It developed under strong Greek influences, evolving from rudimentary adaptations of Hellenistic models to sophisticated expressions of Roman identity, politics, and values, with major genres such as epic poetry, satire, oratory, and historiography dominating its canon. Key periods include the Archaic era (c. 3rdâ2nd centuries BCE), marked by foundational translations and comedies; the Golden Age (c. 80 BCEâ14 CE), renowned for its classical elegance in works by Cicero, Virgil, and Horace; the Silver Age (c. 14â138 CE), characterized by rhetorical complexity in authors like Seneca and Tacitus; Late Antiquity (c. 2ndâ5th centuries CE), blending pagan and Christian themes in texts by Augustine and Jerome; Medieval Latin (c. 5thâ15th centuries), focusing on theology and scholarship; Neo-Latin (15thâ18th centuries), reviving classical forms in Renaissance humanism; and modern Latin (19th centuryâpresent), continuing in scholarly, scientific, and ecclesiastical writing. The Archaic period laid the groundwork for Latin literature, beginning with Livius Andronicus's translation of Homer's Odyssey around 240 BCE, which introduced Greek literary forms to Rome. Pioneering authors like Naevius ( Bellum Punicum), Ennius ( Annales), Plautus (20 extant comedies), Cato the Elder ( Origines), and Terence (6 plays) established epic poetry, comedy, history, and agricultural prose, reflecting Rome's expansion and cultural assimilation during the Republic. Lucretius's philosophical epic De Rerum Natura bridged this era to the Golden Age, using hexameter to expound Epicurean atomism. The Golden Age, coinciding with the late Republic and early Empire under Augustus, represents the zenith of Latin literary achievement, emphasizing harmony, restraint, and moral depth. Cicero's 58 surviving orations and philosophical treatises defined Roman eloquence and rhetoric, while Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico offered concise military history. Poets like Catullus (lyric and epigrams), Virgil ( Aeneid, an epic linking Rome's founding to Trojan legend over 10 years of composition), Horace ( Odes), Propertius, Tibullus, and Ovid ( Metamorphoses, a mythological compendium) innovated in elegy, satire, and narrative verse, often patronized by imperial figures and influencing European literature for centuries. Livy's Ab Urbe Condita chronicled Rome's history in 142 books, embodying patriotic historiography. In the Silver Age, literature grew more ornate and introspective amid imperial stability, with Seneca's tragedies exploring Stoic ethics, Lucan's Bellum Civile, Petronius's novel Satyricon, Pliny the Elder's encyclopedic Historia Naturalis (37 books), Persius and Juvenal's satires, Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria on education, Martial's epigrams, Statius's Thebaid, Tacitus's analytical Annales (16 books), Suetonius's De Vita Caesarum, and Apuleius's Golden Ass âthe only surviving Latin novelâhighlighting satire, biography, and prose fiction. Late Antiquity transitioned to Christian dominance, featuring Ambrose's hymns, Jerome's Vulgate Bible translation, Augustine's Confessions and City of God (theological masterpieces blending autobiography and philosophy), and Boethius's The Consolation of Philosophy. Medieval Latin literature, serving the Church and courts, produced religious treatises, hagiographies, and chronicles like Einhard's Life of Charlemagne, alongside Goliardic secular poetry and theological works by Aquinas. Neo-Latin revived classical styles in humanism, with contributions from Petrarch, Erasmus, and Milton, extending Latin's role in science and philosophy until vernacular languages prevailed. Overall, Latin literature's enduring legacy lies in its fusion of Greek heritage with Roman pragmatism, informing law, ethics, and aesthetics across millennia.
